summary: Specifies a RObust Header Compression profile for TCP/IP packets. It compresses TCP headers, including common options like SACK and Timestamps, and works well over links with high error rates and long round-trip times.

plainLanguage.summary: Packages have long address labels that repeat. This shrinks the label to a tiny code after the first time, which helps on slow or leaky wireless links.

subtitle: A robust way to shrink TCP/IP headers over lossy, slow links, including TCP options like SACK and Timestamps.

tldr.problem: Older TCP/IP header compression (CTCP and IPHC) breaks down on lossy links, handles TCP options poorly, and cannot compress SYN and FIN packets.
tldr.mechanism: ROHC-TCP keeps matching contexts at a compressor and a decompressor, sends only the information needed under an optimistic approach, protects every packet with a CRC, and uses optional feedback (ACK, NACK, STATIC-NACK) to adjust.
tldr.outcome: It is profile 0x0006 of the ROHC framework and obsoletes RFC 4996, fixing the SACK compression and clarifying other methods.

facts.label: Base header formats
facts.value: Two sets of eight, plus one common format

today: RFC 6846 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2013. It obsoletes RFC 4996, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Robust TCP Profile
sections.content:
Header compression on low- or medium-speed links for TCP/IP traffic has long been worthwhile, and RFC 4163 adds why robustness matters for TCP. The existing schemes, RFC 1144 and RFC 2507, are limited in how they handle the TCP options field and cannot compress the headers of handshaking packets (SYNs and FINs).

A better scheme must handle loss on the link between compression and decompression points as well as loss before the compressor. It should also compress short-lived TCP transfers and options such as SACK and Timestamps efficiently. Rarely used options do not need compressing and can pass through unchanged.

RFC 6846 defines a TCP/IP profile for the ROHC framework of RFC 5795, called ROHC-TCP. Its profile identifier is 0x0006.
sections.plainLanguage: Old shortcuts for TCP labels stopped working when a message got lost on the way. This one is built to keep working even when things go missing.

sections.title: What Went Wrong With Older Schemes
sections.content:
Both older schemes send only the differences from the previous header. CTCP (RFC 1144) works well over reliable links, but one lost packet desynchronizes compressor and decompressor. The TCP receiver then discards the rest of the window because of a checksum error, which stops fast retransmit from triggering, and the compressor must wait for a TCP timeout.

IPHC (RFC 2507) adds a local repair mechanism called TWICE and a link-layer request for a full header. TWICE assumes only the sequence number changes by a constant step, which is not always true with Timestamps and SACK. The full-header request needs a feedback channel and does not do well on links with long round-trip times. For IPHC, any change in the options field makes the whole field uncompressible, and for CTCP it effectively disables compression.

The profile builds on a classification of header fields from RFC 4413. Most fields seldom or never change. The ones needing smarter handling include the IPv4 Identification (16 bits), TCP Sequence Number (32 bits), Acknowledgment Number (32 bits), Window (16 bits) and options such as MSS, Window Scale, SACK Permitted, SACK and Timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: If the old shortcut missed even one message, both sides got confused and nobody could read anything until a long timeout passed.

sections.title: How the Compressor and Decompressor Cooperate
sections.content:
The compressor starts by assuming the decompressor knows nothing about a new flow and sends Initialization and Refresh (IR) packets. It may instead use an IR-CR packet to reuse context from another flow. As confidence grows, it moves to smaller Compressed (CO) packets.

The core rule is the optimistic approach. If a field changes, the compressor MUST keep using a packet type that carries that field until it is confident the decompressor has received at least one packet with the new value, and SHOULD choose the smallest header that does so. Until a feedback channel exists, the compressor SHOULD periodically fall back and send IR and/or IR-DYN packets.

Feedback is optional, but once a decompressor uses it for a context, ROHC-TCP assumes it will be used throughout. A NACK tells the compressor to assume only the static part is valid and to resend dynamic information. A STATIC-NACK tells it to assume the decompressor has no valid context and to resend everything through an IR packet. The compressor MAY treat an ACK as confidence to move to a higher compression state, but MUST NOT expect ACKs. Feedback is a poor fit where the MSN bits could wrap within one round-trip time; periodic refreshes without feedback suit that case better.
sections.plainLanguage: At first the sender writes out everything. Once it is fairly sure the receiver has it, the sender sends shorter and shorter notes. If the receiver says it is lost, the sender writes more again.

sections.title: The Decompressor's Three States
sections.content:
The decompressor has three states: No Context (NC), Static Context (SC) and Full Context (FC). It starts in NC, and any successfully decompressed packet moves it to FC. It normally stays in FC, and only repeated failures push it downward.

Every IR and IR-DYN header is checked with a CRC-8, and other packets are checked with the CRC they carry. If verification fails, the packet MUST NOT be delivered to upper layers and the context MUST NOT be updated. In NC only IR and IR-CR packets can be decompressed. In SC, packets with 8-bit CRC coverage (IR, IR-DYN) or CO packets with a 7-bit CRC can be decompressed. In FC, any packet type may be tried. How context damage is detected is left to implementations. The decompressor should limit how often it sends feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver knows nothing at first, then learns the unchanging parts, then learns everything. If lots of notes fail to make sense, it steps back a level and asks for more help.

sections.title: Control Fields, Chains and TCP Options
sections.content:
ROHC-TCP creates a control field, the Master Sequence Number (MSN), because no TCP header field can serve. The compressor increments it by one per packet. The full 16-bit MSN is sent in IR and IR-DYN packets, and LSB-encoded in CO packets. It tells feedback which packet is acknowledged and lets sequential fields like the IP-ID be inferred. The IP-ID can be sequential, sequential byte-swapped, random or constant zero. Only the innermost IP header may be sequential.

Header information is grouped into chains: static, dynamic, replicate (only in IR-CR) and irregular (only in CO packets). Fields such as the IPv4 checksum, IPv4 Total Length, IPv6 Payload Length and TCP Data Offset take zero bits because the decompressor recomputes them. The sequence number can be sent scaled by the payload size, and the acknowledgment number scaled by an explicitly sent ack_stride.

TCP options use list compression. Each option gets a table index, and the table holds up to 16 items. Indexes 0 to 6 are reserved for NOP, EOL, MSS, Window Scale, Timestamp, SACK-Permitted and SACK, and 7 to 15 are for generic options. When the list structure and content are unchanged, nothing about the list is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender numbers every note so the receiver can say which one it got. Parts of the label that rarely change go in a small shared notebook, and only the page number is sent after that.

sections.title: Packet Types and Feedback Formats
sections.content:
There are three packet types: IR (static and dynamic parts of the context), IR-CR (a reference to a base context plus whatever differs) and CO (irregularities in the header; all CO packets carry a CRC and can update the context). The IR type octet is 11111101, IR-DYN is 11111000 and IR-CR is 11111100. The profile field in all three is 0x06.

The CO packets use two sets of eight base header formats plus one common format. The "sequential" set is for a sequential IP-ID and the "random" set for the rest. Formats carry the sequence number, scaled sequence number, acknowledgment number, both, or the window, and format 8 carries rarely changing fields. Each base header has an LSB-encoded MSN, the TCP Push flag and a CRC. A 3-bit CRC is used unless the header can change control fields, in which case a 7-bit CRC is used.

Feedback comes in two shapes. FEEDBACK-1 is a single MSN octet and is always an ACK. FEEDBACK-2 has an Acktype, MSN, an 8-bit CRC and optional feedback options. The compressor MUST discard a FEEDBACK-2 whose CRC does not match. Options include REJECT, MSN-NOT-VALID, MSN and CONTEXT_MEMORY.
sections.plainLanguage: There are a few kinds of notes: a full introduction, a quick copy of an earlier introduction, and tiny updates. The receiver can answer with a thumbs up or a request for more detail.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 4996
sections.content:
RFC 6846 revises RFC 4996 and is mostly backwards-compatible with it, except for two cases that did not interoperate. First, SACK compression in RFC 4996 assumed SACK blocks were in sorted order, so unsorted blocks could be impossible to compress. The SACK compression changed, and so did the bits on the wire. Second, ESP NULL header compression was deprecated because of interoperability problems with needing information from the trailer.

The other changes are described as non-functional. Several descriptions in the formal notation were corrected (sequential IP-ID compression, scaled encodings, external arguments), without changing the bits on the wire. Errata for RFC 4996 were also corrected.
sections.plainLanguage: The older version had a mistake in how it shortened one kind of note. This version fixes it, and cleans up the instructions without changing the rest.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malfunctioning or malicious compressor could cause the decompressor to rebuild packets that do not match the originals but still have valid IP and TCP headers, and possibly valid TCP checksums. End-to-end authentication and integrity mechanisms can detect this, and the internal CRC lowers the chance it goes unnoticed.

Denial of service is possible if an intruder injects bogus IR, CO or FEEDBACK packets and so reduces compression efficiency. The RFC adds that an intruder able to inject arbitrary packets at the link layer raises further security issues that dwarf those of header compression.
sections.plainLanguage: A cheating helper could rebuild a label wrongly, and a troublemaker could send fake notes to slow things down. Checks at the ends of the trip help catch it.
